## Modding Super Mario Galaxy with Nebula

Nebula is Super Mario Galaxy rebuilt as a native program. LumaLink makes mods for it: it converts what people have already made, and it builds new ones. A mod is one `.luma` file that works on every version of the game and every device.

A mod can change files, levels, objects, the player's physics, power-ups, the star count, the story's order, music, text, shaders and cutscenes, and add new enemies, characters and galaxies. Most of it needs no code; the plugin interface covers the rest.

| Example | Shows |
|---|---|
| `new-text` | Messages in several languages |
| `interface-picture` | A picture in the game's interface, from a PNG |
| `stage-music` | New music in a stage, per mission and per area |
| `new-cutscene` | A whole cutscene from tables |
| `one-health`, `coin-kills`, `boss-music`, `double-jump` | Small plugins |
| `achievements` | The mod's own achievements, on the game's board: by events, and by its code |
| `gecko-*` (20 of them) | Popular Gecko codes done natively: moon jump, infinite health, Mario's size, no spin cooldown and the rest ([the list](#p-tutorials-15-converting--popular-gecko-codes)) |
| `little-boss` | A three-phase boss: model, music, placement, attacks |
| `gold-flower` | A new power-up: its item, model, particles, sounds, spin animation, fire damage and higher jump |
| `new-galaxy` | A whole galaxy: planet, ground, gravity, a new enemy, stars, a cutscene with a glTF camera |
| `new-npc` | A new character made like a Toad, with its own model and talk |
| `new-talk` | A branching yes/no talk on one of the game's Toads |
| `new-voice` | The player's voices from the mod's own sounds |
| `evening-light` | A stage's light changed by a table merge: warm evening colours on Good Egg |
| `far-camera` | A stage's camera changed by a merge: further back and wider |
| `quick-star-get` | Timing by tunables: the star's ending sooner |
| `glowing-lantern` | A hand-written shader for a model's material (`custom-shaders`) |
| `coin-bank` | A plugin that keeps numbers and words across plays (its own store) |
| `goomba-tempo` | A plugin that changes the game's objects' animations, with an option |
| `first-person` | The whole game through Mario's eyes: a camera of the plugin's own, handed back for cutscenes and talks ([tutorial 18](#p-tutorials-18-first-person)) |


<a id="p-using-mods"></a>

<a id="p-using-mods--using-mods"></a>

## Using mods

<a id="p-using-mods--installing-one"></a>

### Installing one

**A `.luma` file.** Double-click it, or in Nebula's settings choose Mods, then Import file. It appears on, at the top of the list, and applies when Nebula restarts (the page offers the restart). A mod with its own code asks first.

**A mod as you downloaded it** (a zip, 7z, rar or a folder, made for the Wii). Open LumaLink, drop it on the window, tick it, and press Convert. Open the `.luma` it makes.

**On a phone.** Move the `.luma` to the phone and import it from the app. It's on from the next start. A raw mod folder can't be used on a phone: convert it on a computer first.

<a id="p-using-mods--the-list"></a>

### The list

The Mods page has two lists: Off and On (the higher one wins). Mods apply from the bottom of the On list up, so the one on top wins where two change the same file, texture or setting. Drag a mod to move it, or select it, press A (Space on a keyboard) to pick it up, move it with the arrows (left turns it off, right on) and press A again to put it down. Files many mods add to, such as a level's objects, keep everyone's additions. Text, settings and table rows follow the same order: the higher mod's word is the one used.

The line under a selected mod says what it changes and where it overlaps another mod: OVERRIDES: {NAME} (3 FILES) means it wins those, OVERRIDDEN BY: {NAME} means the other one does.

Changes wait until you press Apply. Mods that change the game's files apply when the game restarts, and Apply offers to restart; texture packs and movies apply at once.

<a id="p-using-mods--a-mods-page"></a>

### A mod's page

Select a mod and press Details. Its page shows:

| Line | What it is |
|---|---|
| Status | On (its place in the list) or off; left and right turn it on or off. The line under it says why a mod can't be used. |
| Changes | What kinds of things it changes: files, settings, textures, movies, code. The line under it lists every overlap. |
| Version, By, License, Website | What its maker wrote in the mod. |
| Folder | Its folder in the mods folder. |
| Options | Its choices, the text it shows in a language it lacks, a texture pack's categories. |

About shows its description, then its icon and pictures, a page at a time. Remove removes it (to the Recycle Bin on Windows) after asking; a mod the game started with is in use: turn it off, restart, then remove it.

<a id="p-using-mods--updating"></a>

### Updating

Importing a `.luma` whose `id` is already in the mods folder replaces that mod, whatever its folder is called, and keeps its place, its options and its saves. The message says which: Updated: {name} ({old} to {new}), Older version, or Replaced (the same version). A different mod that happens to have the same folder name is left alone; the new one gets a folder of its own. On Windows, if another program has a file of the mod open, the update waits and takes its place at the next start. If Nebula closes during an import, the next start puts the mod back as it was and clears what was half copied.

Two folders holding the same mod (a copy made by hand) can't both be on: the lower one says ANOTHER COPY OF THIS MOD IS ON.

<a id="p-using-mods--mods-with-code"></a>

### Mods with code

Some mods hold their own compiled code. The game asks before that code first runs, and again whenever it changes. It runs with the same rights as the game, so turn it on only for mods you trust. If the game crashes with mods' code on, the crash report names the mods, and on Windows the next run starts with every mod's code off.

<a id="p-using-mods--saves"></a>

### Saves

A mod says which saves it plays on.

| It says | You get |
|---|---|
| `shared` | Your normal saves |
| `own` | Saves of its own, starting new or from what the mod brings |
| `copy` | Saves of its own, starting as a copy of yours. Yours stay as they are |

A mod that adds a galaxy always has its own, since a save's shape follows the list of galaxies; two such mods play on the higher one's. Saves of its own outlast updating or removing the mod.

<a id="p-using-mods--when-a-mod-cant-be-used"></a>

### When a mod can't be used

It stays on the list, off, with one line saying why. See [Messages](#p-reference--17-messages-and-what-they-mean).

<a id="p-using-mods--when-somethings-wrong"></a>

### When something's wrong

- **A new line in the log says `mods: left out:`.** Part of the mod couldn't be used, and the rest is running. The line says which part and why. The log is `nebula.log` in the settings folder; every mod line it can hold is in [Messages](#p-reference--in-the-log).
- **It crashes.** Turn off the mods one at a time, starting from the top of the list, to find which one. If it's a plugin, the crash report names it.
- **Sounds or shaders take a moment the first time.** A mod's shaders are built on your device on first use, with a progress screen. After that, it's instant.


<a id="p-start-here"></a>

<a id="p-start-here--start-here"></a>

## Start here

Ten minutes, and you'll have changed the game. You need Nebula with your game imported, and LumaLink.

<a id="p-start-here--1-make-a-project"></a>

### 1. Make a project

```console
lumalink new "My First Mod"
```

```text
My First Mod/
├── luma.json                what the mod is
└── layers/base/
    ├── files/               files by their place in the game
    └── textures/            replacement textures
```

`luma.json` already says enough to be a mod:

```json
{
  "format": 1,
  "id": "my-first-mod",
  "name": "My First Mod",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "game": "RMG",
  "layers": [ { "path": "layers/base" } ]
}
```

<a id="p-start-here--2-change-how-high-mario-jumps"></a>

### 2. Change how high Mario jumps

Add this to the layer:

```json
"layers": [ {
  "path": "layers/base",
  "player_constants": { "mario": { "mJumpHeight": [null, null, 60.0] } }
} ]
```

`mJumpHeight` is a list of nine, for each kind of jump. The third is the triple jump, 36 in the game. `null` keeps the game's number. There are 493 numbers like this: see [Player numbers](#p-reference-player-numbers).

<a id="p-start-here--3-rename-a-galaxy"></a>

### 3. Rename a galaxy

Add this beside `layers`:

```json
"text": { "GalaxyName_EggStarGalaxy": "The Very Good Egg" }
```

<a id="p-start-here--4-give-mario-six-health-from-the-start-and-a-thousand-lives"></a>

### 4. Give Mario six health from the start, and a thousand lives

```json
"requires": ["tunables"],
"layers": [ {
  "path": "layers/base",
  "player_constants": { "mario": { "mJumpHeight": [null, null, 60.0] } },
  "tunables": { "GameRules.cPlayerHealth": 6, "GameDataPlayerStatus.cMaxPlayerLeft": 999, "GameDataPlayerStatus.cStartingPlayerLeft": 100 }
} ]
```

<a id="p-start-here--5-check-it-and-run-it"></a>

### 5. Check it and run it

```console
lumalink check "My First Mod"
lumalink run "My First Mod"
```

`check` lists every mistake it can find. `run` builds the `.luma` and opens it in Nebula's Mods page. Turn it on, press Apply, and start a game.

To make the file without opening it: `lumalink pack "My First Mod"`.

<a id="p-start-here--what-next"></a>

### What next

Anything you can see or hear is a file you can replace: [textures](#p-tutorials-01-textures), [models](#p-tutorials-02-models), [music](#p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound). Levels are [tables of objects](#p-tutorials-03-levels). New objects and whole galaxies take [no code](#p-tutorials-08-new-objects). When data can't do it, [plugins](#p-tutorials-10-first-plugin) can do anything the game can.

To see how anyone else did something:

```console
lumalink unpack "Some Mod.luma" -o folder
```

To see what the game has:

```console
lumalink list objects --filter Coin
lumalink files StageData/EggStarGalaxy --game path/to/game.pak
lumalink extract StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo --game path/to/game.pak -o out
```


<a id="p-concepts"></a>

<a id="p-concepts--how-mods-work"></a>

## How mods work

<a id="p-concepts--the-pieces"></a>

### The pieces

| Piece | What it is | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| **Nebula** | The game, built to run natively. It reads `.luma` files | Every device |
| **LumaLink** | The converter and modding tool | A computer |
| **`.luma`** | One mod in one file, for every version of the game and every device | Anywhere |
| **Plugin** | A mod's own compiled code, inside a `.luma` | Inside Nebula |

A mod is made once. Nothing about it depends on one build of Nebula: the game prepares what it needs when the mod is first used, and again if its own needs change.

<a id="p-concepts--inside-a-luma"></a>

### Inside a `.luma`

A zip file with `luma.json` as its first entry. Any zip tool can make one, and `lumalink unpack` opens one.

```text
My Mod.luma
├── luma.json                what the mod is
├── icon.png                 optional, square
├── layers/
│   └── base/
│       ├── files/           files by their place in the game
│       ├── merge/           what it adds to, or changes in, files many mods share
│       ├── textures/        replacement textures
│       └── movies/          replacement videos
├── save/                    optional, starting files for its own saves
└── plugins/                 optional, the mod's code
```

<a id="p-concepts--the-ways-to-change-the-game"></a>

### The ways to change the game

From the simplest to the most powerful. Use the first one that does what you want.

| Way | What it changes | Two mods can both do it? |
|---|---|---|
| **Tunables** (`tunables`) | Every tuning number and rule: health, lives, caps, speeds, timers | Yes, the higher wins |
| **Player numbers** (`player_constants`) | How the player moves, how long power-ups last | Yes, per number |
| **Rows** (`music`, `text`, `event_flags`, `stages`, `object_classes`, ...) | The game's tables: what plays where, what opens what | Yes, per row |
| **Merge** (`merge/`) | Rows in levels and tables: add, change, remove | Yes, all kept |
| **Files** (`files/`) | Anything that's a file: models, textures, levels, sounds | The higher replaces |
| **Plugin, stable interface** | Anything, through 140 plain C calls and events. Survives Nebula updates | Yes |
| **Plugin, game's headers and hooks** | Any function of the game | Yes, in a chain |

<a id="p-concepts--layers-and-options"></a>

### Layers and options

A layer is a folder and when to use it. Layers apply in order, and later ones win. Everything that differs by version, language, device or the player's choice is a layer, so one file carries it all.

```json
"layers": [
  { "path": "layers/base" },
  { "path": "layers/hard", "when": { "option": { "difficulty": ["hard"] } } },
  { "path": "layers/japanese", "when": { "version": ["J"] } }
]
```

Everything a mod can say can go in a layer, so an option can turn on a galaxy, a track, a setting or a line of text.

<a id="p-concepts--with-no-mods-on"></a>

### With no mods on

Nebula with no mods is the game as it always was. Some changes apply only once any mod is on: every power-up's model and every sound bank are then loaded on every stage, so an object works wherever a mod puts it. That costs a little memory, and no one playing without mods pays for it.

<a id="p-concepts--why-theres-no-code-from-the-wii"></a>

### Why there's no code from the Wii

Wii mods change the game by writing over its program. Nebula isn't that program. So LumaLink reads each write for what it changes in the game, and turns it into a setting: a write over the player's table becomes `player_constants`, a write over the object table becomes `object_changes`. Any mod writing any value there works, since the value is read out of the bytes. No code from a mod's patch ever runs. A write that LumaLink can't read stays on a list, and everything else in the mod still works. See [What conversion reads](#p-reference--4-what-conversion-does).


<a id="p-guide"></a>

<a id="p-guide--making-mods-for-nebula"></a>

## Making mods for Nebula

This guide starts from nothing and ends with a galaxy of your own. Every example here has been built with LumaLink and run in the game. The ones in [`examples/`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples) are complete projects: copy one and change it.

You need LumaLink, your game imported into Nebula (Nebula made a `game.pak` from your disc), and for code, [clang](https://llvm.org). The full rules of the file are in [format.md](#p-format). The plugin interface is in [plugins.md](#p-plugins).

<a id="p-guide--your-first-mod"></a>

### Your first mod

```console
lumalink new "My Mod"
```

This makes a folder:

```text
My Mod/
├── luma.json                what the mod is
└── layers/base/
    ├── files/               files by their place in the game
    └── textures/            replacement textures
```

A file in `layers/base/files/` takes the place of the game's file at the same path. To change a model, put yours at `layers/base/files/ObjectData/Kuribo.arc`.

When it's ready:

```console
lumalink check "My Mod"
lumalink pack "My Mod"
```

`check` lists every mistake it can find. `pack` writes `My Mod.luma`. Open that file in Nebula: Settings, Mods, Import. Then turn the mod on and press Apply.

To see what's inside anyone's mod, run `lumalink unpack "Some Mod.luma" -o folder`.

<a id="p-guide--changing-one-file-inside-an-archive"></a>

### Changing one file inside an archive

The game keeps most things in `.arc` archives. You don't have to bring a whole archive to change one file in it. Name the archive as a folder:

```text
layers/base/files/ObjectData/Kuribo.arc/kuribo.bdl
```

The rest of the archive comes from the player's own game. So your mod holds only your work, and it doesn't carry any of the game's files.

<a id="p-guide--models-and-animations"></a>

### Models and animations

Put a `.glb` or `.gltf` where the game's model goes:

```text
layers/base/files/ObjectData/MyThing.arc/mything.glb
```

Nebula turns it into the game's own model when the player applies the mod, with one animation file for each animation in it. Materials get their shaders automatically. Vertex skinning works, up to the game's limit of joints.

You can also use the game's own formats (`.bdl`, `.bmd`, `.bck`, and so on) from any tool that writes them.

<a id="p-guide--textures"></a>

### Textures

Three ways, depending on what you're changing.

| You want to change | Do this |
|---|---|
| Any texture, wherever it's used | A texture pack: `tex1_` files in `layers/base/textures/` |
| A texture file in an object's archive | `layers/base/files/ObjectData/Thing.arc/name.png` becomes `name.bti` |
| A picture in the game's interface | `layers/base/files/LayoutData/CoinCounter.arc/timg/name.png` becomes `name.tpl` |

See [`examples/interface-picture`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/interface-picture).

<a id="p-guide--music"></a>

### Music

To replace one of the game's tracks, put a `.wav` or `.ogg` with the same name in `layers/base/files/AudioRes/Stream/`.

A new track is a file with a row in `luma.json`:

```json
"music": [{
  "name": "MyTheme",
  "file": "AudioRes/Stream/MyTheme.ogg",
  "stages": [{ "stage": "EggStarGalaxy" }]
}]
```

A row with `"scenario": 3` is for that mission. A row with `"change_area": 1` is what a `ChangeBgmCube` with that `Obj_arg1` starts. See [`examples/stage-music`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/stage-music). Code can start a track too, as [`examples/boss-music`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/boss-music) does.

Loops come from the file: a WAV's `smpl` chunk, an Ogg's `LOOPSTART` and `LOOPEND` comments. Without them the whole track loops.

<a id="p-guide--text"></a>

### Text

Any message in the game, by its id, in as many languages as you like:

```json
"text": {
  "GalaxyName_EggStarGalaxy": { "default": "The Very First Galaxy", "fr": "La toute première galaxie" }
}
```

See [`examples/new-text`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/new-text).

<a id="p-guide--adding-to-levels-and-tables"></a>

### Adding to levels and tables

Replacing a whole file means only one mod can change it. A layer's `merge/` folder adds rows instead, so any number of mods can add to the same level.

```text
layers/base/merge/StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo.json
```

```json
{ "rows": [ { "name": "Coin", "l_id": 900, "pos_x": 0, "pos_y": 100, "pos_z": 0, "scale_x": 1, "scale_y": 1, "scale_z": 1 } ] }
```

A column you leave out is zero or empty. In placement tables, "no switch" and "no argument" are `-1`, so write those out: `"SW_A": -1`.

Particles add the same way: see "Adding to shared files" in [format.md](#p-format).

To make a table that doesn't exist yet, write `Name.bcsv.json` in `files/`. The kind of each column comes from its values. Say it yourself for a float whose values are all whole numbers, or for a column with no values yet:

```json
{ "columns": { "Speed": "float" }, "rows": [ { "Name": "Fast", "Speed": 2 } ] }
```

<a id="p-guide--in-game-cutscenes"></a>

### In-game cutscenes

A cutscene is data: a `DemoGroup` placed in a level, and its sheets in `ObjectData/DemoSheet.arc`. [`examples/new-cutscene`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/new-cutscene) makes a whole one with no code and none of the game's files:

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `files/ObjectData/DemoSheet.arc/demomycutscene/demomycutscenetime.bcsv.json` | Its parts, and how long each lasts, in frames |
| `...player.bcsv.json` | The player's animation in each part |
| `...sound.bcsv.json` | Music and sounds in each part |
| `...wipe.bcsv.json` | Fades in and out |
| `...camera.bcsv.json` | Cameras |
| `...action.bcsv.json` | What each object in the cutscene does |
| `merge/StageData/.../demoobjinfo.json` | The `DemoGroup`: its name, its sheets' name, and the switch that starts it |
| `merge/StageData/.../areaobjinfo.json` | A `SwitchCube` that turns that switch on when the player walks in |

Leave out any sheet you don't need. A wrong name in a sheet (a part, an animation, a position, a sound, a wipe, a cast) does nothing: the cutscene carries on without it.

Code can tell when a cutscene starts and ends: see [`native/plugin_sdk/examples/cutscene_log`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/nebula/tree/main/native/plugin_sdk/examples/cutscene_log).

To replace one of the game's own, change its sheet the same way.

<a id="p-guide--movies"></a>

### Movies

To replace a movie, put a video in `layers/base/movies/` or a `.thp` in `files/MovieData/`. A plugin can play a movie of the mod's in any scene:

```c
game->play_movie("MovieData/MyMovie.thp");
```

<a id="p-guide--lumas"></a>

### Lumas

Each kind is placed as an object, by its name.

| Name | What it is | Set in its row |
|---|---|---|
| `Tico`, `TicoBaby` | A Luma that talks | `MessageId` for what it says |
| `TicoComet` | A Luma for the comet | |
| `TicoShop` | Sells for star bits | `Obj_arg0`: the price |
| `TicoFat` | Hungry, gives an item when fed | `Obj_arg0`: the item (0: 1-up, 1: life mushroom). `Obj_arg1`: how much it eats |
| `TicoGalaxy` | Hungry, opens a galaxy when fed | `Obj_arg1`: how much it eats. `Obj_arg7`: its slot. `CommonPath_ID`: where it flies. A `GroupId` shared with a launch star |
| `TicoRail` | Moves along a path | `CommonPath_ID` |
| `TicoReading` | Listens in the library | |
| `TicoStarRing` | Launches you to a galaxy | `Obj_arg0`: which |
| `TicoAstro` | In the Observatory, by green stars | `Obj_arg0`, `Obj_arg2` |
| `TicoDomeLecture` | The dome's lecture | Belongs in a `DemoGroup` |
| `CollectTico` + `StrayTico` | Gather the lost Lumas for a star | In one group, with a `PowerStar` row in the mission |

For a new look, give a kind a new model file: `ObjectData/TicoShop.arc`.

Row details follow the game's own levels: `lumalink unpack` a mod or read the disc's with a level editor.

<a id="p-guide--your-own-galaxy"></a>

### Your own galaxy

A galaxy beside the game's is its files and a row:

```text
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy/MyGalaxyScenario.arc
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc
```

```json
"galaxies": [{
  "name": "MyGalaxy",
  "dome": 1,
  "map_position": [-60, -100],
  "hungry_luma": { "slot": 7, "star_bits": 400 }
}],
"save": { "mode": "own" },
"text": {
  "GalaxyName_MyGalaxy": "My Galaxy",
  "ScenarioName_MyGalaxy1": "The First Star"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dome` | Its dome, 1 to 6. 0: on the grand map |
| `map_position` | Where its icon goes, right and up from the middle of the page. The game makes the icon |
| `hungry_luma` | The Luma that opens it. Place a `TicoGalaxy` in the Observatory with its `Obj_arg7` at this slot, through `merge/` |
| `save` | A galaxy needs its own saves. `check` tells you if you forget |

Your levels are level files, from a level editor such as Whitehole. Your stars are rows in the scenario archive's `ScenarioData`. Bosses and enemies are placed objects: new looks are new models, new behaviour is a plugin, as [`examples/little-boss`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/little-boss) shows.

To rearrange the game's own journey, as Kaizo does, see "The game's progression" in [format.md](#p-format).

<a id="p-guide--options-for-the-player"></a>

### Options for the player

```json
"options": [{
  "id": "difficulty", "name": "Difficulty", "default": "normal",
  "choices": [ { "id": "normal", "name": "Normal" }, { "id": "hard", "name": "Hard" } ]
}],
"layers": [
  { "path": "layers/base" },
  { "path": "layers/hard", "when": { "option": { "difficulty": ["hard"] } } }
]
```

Players choose on the Mods page, and the choice lasts through updates to the mod.

<a id="p-guide--saves"></a>

### Saves

| `save.mode` | What the player gets |
|---|---|
| `shared` (the default) | Their normal saves |
| `own` | Saves of its own, starting new or from `save.path` |
| `copy` | Saves of its own, starting from a copy of theirs |

`save.tag` names the family: mods with the same tag share saves. `save.player_can_change` lets the player choose on the Mods page.

<a id="p-guide--your-own-shaders"></a>

### Your own shaders

Materials build their own shaders, so most mods never think about this. For a special effect, run `lumalink shader model.glb -o folder`, change the HLSL it writes, and name it:

```json
"requires": ["custom-shaders"],
"layers": [{ "path": "layers/base", "materials": { "WaterSurface": "layers/base/shaders/my-water.hlsl" } }]
```

The game builds it for Direct3D 12 and Vulkan on the player's device.

<a id="p-guide--code"></a>

### Code

When data can't do it, write a plugin.

```console
lumalink new "My Mod" --plugin
```

```c
/* Any hit is the last one. */
#include "nebula_mod_api.h"

static const NebulaModApi* game;

static int32_t stage_frame(const NebulaModEventData* data, void* user) {
    (void)user;
    if (game->value(NEBULA_VALUE_LIFE) > 1) {
        game->set_value(NEBULA_SET_LIFE, 1);
    }
    return data->value;
}

NEBULA_PLUGIN_ENTRY(api, self) {
    game = api;
    game->subscribe(NEBULA_MOD_EVENT_STAGE_FRAME, stage_frame, 0);
}
```

Build it with `build.cmd`. The game asks the player before it first runs a mod's code, and again if the code changes.

| Example | What it shows |
|---|---|
| [`one-health`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/one-health) | Reading and setting the player's state |
| [`coin-kills`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/coin-kills) | Events |
| [`achievements`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/achievements) | The mod's own achievements: three unlocked by events, one by its code |
| [`boss-music`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/boss-music) | Starting and stopping music |
| [`double-jump`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/double-jump) | A new move for the player: the buttons, gravity, an animation |
| [`little-boss`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/little-boss) | A new enemy: its model, music, health, placement and what it does |
| [`coin-bank`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/coin-bank) | Keeping numbers and words across plays (`store_get`, `store_set_text`), a message when the player has control |
| [`goomba-tempo`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/goomba-tempo) | Every object of a kind (`find_actor`), its animation's speed, an option |
| [`first-person`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/first-person) | A camera of the plugin's own every frame (`set_camera`, `set_camera_near`), the player's model hidden, the game's cameras back for cutscenes ([tutorial 18](#p-tutorials-18-first-person)) |
| [`pulse`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/nebula/tree/main/native/plugin_sdk/examples/pulse) | A new object with the game's headers, and a hook |
| [`cube`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/nebula/tree/main/native/plugin_sdk/examples/cube) | A new object with the stable interface and a glTF model |

A new object is one call, `register_object`, and then levels place it by its name. A new power-up is `add_power_up`. A new Mario move is the player's buttons and `jump_player` or `play`, or a hook on the player's functions. All of it is in [plugins.md](#p-plugins).

<a id="p-guide--publishing"></a>

### Publishing

Put the `.luma` anywhere people can download it. Before you do:

- Run `lumalink check` on the finished file.
- Give it a real `version`. A file with the same `id` and a higher version updates the mod and keeps the player's settings.
- Bring only your own work. Name archives as folders so the player's game supplies the rest.
- If your mod has code, build it for each device it should run on.


# Tutorials

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures--change-a-texture"></a>

## Change a texture

Three ways, depending on what you're changing.

| You want to change | Do this |
|---|---|
| A texture wherever it's used, by its look | A texture pack: `tex1_` files in `layers/base/textures/` |
| A texture file in one object's archive | `layers/base/files/ObjectData/Thing.arc/name.png` |
| A picture in the interface | `layers/base/files/LayoutData/CoinCounter.arc/timg/name.png` |

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures--a-texture-pack"></a>

### A texture pack

Any Dolphin texture pack works as it is: its `tex1_` files go in `layers/base/textures/`, in any folders. PNG and DDS both work, mipmaps too, at any size. To make one, dump the game's textures in Dolphin, edit what you want, and keep only those.

A pack for the Wii version converts without changes: drop it on LumaLink. Players can turn a pack's categories on and off on the Mods page.

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures--one-objects-texture"></a>

### One object's texture

```text
layers/base/files/ObjectData/Kuribo.arc/kuribo_body.png
```

A folder named as an archive changes that archive file by file, and the rest comes from the player's own game. The PNG becomes the game's `.bti` when the player applies the mod.

To see what an archive holds:

```console
lumalink files ObjectData/Kuribo.arc --game path/to/game.pak
```

Names are the files in the archive, in any case, without the ending.

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures--a-picture-in-the-interface"></a>

### A picture in the interface

The interface keeps its pictures in another form, in a folder named `timg`. A PNG there becomes that form, under the name of the picture it replaces. See [`examples/interface-picture`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/interface-picture), which turns the coin counter's coin and × blue.

```text
layers/base/files/LayoutData/CoinCounter.arc/timg/myiconcoin.png
```

`lumalink files LayoutData/CoinCounter.arc --game game.pak` lists an archive's pictures by name.

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures--sizes"></a>

### Sizes

Any size. The game's own limit of 1024 doesn't apply to files from mods. Textures larger than the original simply draw sharper; they don't need the same proportions, but the model's coordinates decide how they map.

<a id="p-tutorials-01-textures--running-it"></a>

### Running it

```console
lumalink check "My Mod"
lumalink run "My Mod"
```


<a id="p-tutorials-02-models"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--change-a-model-and-make-solid-ground"></a>

## Change a model, and make solid ground

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--a-model-from-gltf"></a>

### A model from glTF

Export a `.glb` or `.gltf` from Blender or anything else, and put it where the game's model goes, named as the archive is:

```text
layers/base/files/ObjectData/Kuribo.arc/Kuribo.glb
```

Nebula turns it into the game's own model when the player applies the mod.

| In the file | Becomes |
|---|---|
| Triangles | The model. A metre is 100 of the game's units |
| One colour and one PNG or JPEG per material | The material. The material's name is what [hand-written shaders](#p-reference--15-shaders) use |
| A texture's `KHR_texture_transform` | Its texture matrix |
| A skin | Skinned joints |
| Each animation | Files named after it, beside the model: `.bck` for what it does to the joints, and [for materials](#p-tutorials-02-models--a-material-that-moves) `.bpk`, `.btk` and `.btp` |

A game's object often asks for animations by name. Run `lumalink files ObjectData/Kuribo.arc --game game.pak` to see what the original has, and name yours the same.

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--how-an-animation-plays"></a>

#### How an animation plays

An animation loops unless its `extras` say otherwise. In Blender, that's a custom property on the action, exported with it:

```json
{ "name": "FlatDown", "extras": { "nebula": { "play": "once" } }, "channels": [ ... ] }
```

| `play` | The animation |
|---|---|
| `loop` (or none) | Starts again at its end |
| `once` | Stops on its last frame |
| `once_then_first` | Plays once, then shows its first frame |
| `there_and_back` | Plays once forwards, then backwards |
| `loop_there_and_back` | Forwards and backwards, over and over |

A model standing in for one of the game's ([a new object](#p-tutorials-08-new-objects)) plays each animation the original has as the original's does, whatever this says. Code that waits for an animation's end (a squashed Goomba waits for `FlatDown`) needs it to play once.

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--a-material-that-moves"></a>

#### A material that moves

An animation can change materials as well as joints, through `KHR_animation_pointer`:

| The animation moves | Becomes | For |
|---|---|---|
| `/materials/<n>/pbrMetallicRoughness/baseColorFactor` | `.bpk`, the material's colour | A flash, a glow, fading out |
| `/materials/<n>/pbrMetallicRoughness/baseColorTexture/extensions/KHR_texture_transform/offset`, `scale`, `rotation` | `.btk`, its texture's matrix | Flowing water, a scrolling belt, a spinning pattern |

A texture that turns needs equal scales across and up: glTF scales before turning and the game after, which come out the same only then.

Swapping one texture for another (eyes that blink, a face that changes) is the animation's `extras`:

```json
{ "name": "Blink",
  "extras": { "nebula": { "texture_swaps": [ { "material": 0, "keys": [[0, 3], [0.1, 4], [0.2, 3]] } ] } } }
```

Each key is `[second, texture]`: from that second, the material's base colour texture is glTF texture `texture`. The textures swapped in become part of the model even if no material starts with them. That becomes `.btp`.

An animation needs no joints to move: one with only these is only these files. The game's code asks for a material's animations by name as it does the joints': a Goomba's `Blink` is its `.btp`.

You can use the game's own formats too (`.bdl`, `.bmd`, `.bck`, `.btk`, `.brk`, `.bpk`, `.btp`, `.bva`) from any tool that writes them.

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--solid-ground"></a>

### Solid ground

What the player stands on is separate from what they see, so a platform can have a detailed look and a simple shape. Export the simple shape, and name it `.kcl.glb`:

```text
layers/base/files/ObjectData/MyPlatform.arc/MyPlatform.glb        what you see
layers/base/files/ObjectData/MyPlatform.arc/MyPlatform.kcl.glb    what you stand on
```

It becomes the game's `MyPlatform.kcl` and `MyPlatform.pa`. Faces point out the way they do in the model: counter-clockwise from the side you stand on.

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--what-the-surface-is"></a>

#### What the surface is

Each material of the collision model is one kind of surface. Its glTF `extras` set the columns of the game's attribute table:

```json
"materials": [ { "name": "Ice", "extras": { "Floor_code": 3, "Sound_code": 5 } } ]
```

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Floor_code` | What the floor does: slippery, sand, death |
| `Wall_code` | What a wall does |
| `Sound_code` | What steps sound like |
| `Camera_id` | The camera for standing there |
| `Camera_through` | Whether the camera passes through it |

To see which number means what, read what the game's own use: `lumalink extract ObjectData/SomeObject.arc --game game.pak -o out` gives each `.pa` as JSON.

A collision model holds at most 65,534 triangles and 65,536 distinct points: that's the form of the game's file. Past that, split it into parts: many objects, or many zones.

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--an-object-that-uses-it"></a>

### An object that uses it

If you changed a game's object, you're done. For a new one, see [A new object, without code](#p-tutorials-08-new-objects).

<a id="p-tutorials-02-models--mario"></a>

### Mario

Mario's model is `ObjectData/Mario.arc`, Luigi's `ObjectData/Luigi.arc`, and each power-up's body has its own: `BeeMario`, `IceMario`, `HopperMario`, `InvincibleMario` and the Luigi versions. Keep the skeleton: the game's animations move joints by name. A costume mod is usually a texture and a model in those archives, with no code.


<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--change-a-level"></a>

## Change a level

A stage is tables: which objects stand where, what its zones are, where the player starts.

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--where-things-are"></a>

### Where things are

```text
StageData/<Galaxy>/<Galaxy>Scenario.arc      its missions and zones
StageData/<Zone>.arc                         one zone: placement, paths, cameras, gravity
StageData/<Zone>.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo      objects in every mission
StageData/<Zone>.arc/jmp/placement/layera/objinfo      objects when layer A is on
```

Look at one:

```console
lumalink files StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc --game game.pak
lumalink extract StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo --game game.pak -o out
```

That writes the table, and beside it `objinfo.json`, each row as words and numbers.

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--with-a-level-editor"></a>

### With a level editor

Tools such as Whitehole read and write the game's own files. Save your level, and put the archives in `files/`:

```text
layers/base/files/StageData/MyZone.arc
```

Or keep the disc's folders as the tool writes them; LumaLink finds them by their names. This replaces the whole file, so only one mod's survives. For one mod that's fine.

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--with-merge-add-change-remove"></a>

### With `merge/`: add, change, remove

A file in a layer's `merge/` folder edits a table, and any number of mods can edit one table. The path goes inside the archive, and the name ends in `.json`.

```text
layers/base/merge/StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo.json
```

```json
{
  "remove": [ { "name": "EarthenPipe" } ],
  "change": [
    { "where": { "name": "SuperSpinDriver" }, "set": { "scale_x": 2.0, "scale_y": 2.0, "scale_z": 2.0 } }
  ],
  "rows": [
    {
      "name": "Coin", "l_id": 900,
      "pos_x": -2200, "pos_y": -12700, "pos_z": -14500,
      "dir_x": 0, "dir_y": 0, "dir_z": 0,
      "scale_x": 1, "scale_y": 1, "scale_z": 1,
      "Obj_arg0": -1, "Obj_arg1": -1, "Obj_arg2": -1, "Obj_arg3": -1,
      "Obj_arg4": -1, "Obj_arg5": -1, "Obj_arg6": -1, "Obj_arg7": -1,
      "SW_A": -1, "SW_B": -1, "SW_APPEAR": -1, "SW_DEAD": -1, "SW_SLEEP": -1,
      "CommonPath_ID": -1, "ClippingGroupId": -1, "GroupId": -1, "DemoGroupId": -1,
      "MapParts_ID": -1, "ViewGroupId": -1, "CameraSetId": -1, "CastId": -1,
      "MessageId": -1, "ShapeModelNo": -1
    }
  ]
}
```

They run in that order: remove, change, add. A row that matches nothing is not an error, since another mod may have taken it. See [Tables](#p-reference--8-levels-and-tables).

In placement tables, "no switch" and "no argument" are `-1`, so write those out. A column you leave out is zero, which means "switch number 0": a real one.

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--what-a-row-means"></a>

### What a row means

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | The object: see [Objects](#p-reference-objects) |
| `l_id` | Its number, unique in the table. Use high numbers for your own, 3000 and up |
| `pos_*`, `dir_*`, `scale_*` | Where it is, turned in degrees, its size |
| `Obj_arg0`..`7` | Numbers that mean what the object says |
| `SW_A`, `SW_B`, `SW_APPEAR`, `SW_DEAD`, `SW_SLEEP` | Switches: how objects talk to each other |
| `CommonPath_ID` | Its rail |
| `MessageId` | What it says |
| `GroupId`, `ClippingGroupId` | Objects that belong together |

The easiest way to learn an object's arguments: find one in a level with `extract`, and copy its row.

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--missions-and-layers"></a>

### Missions and layers

A galaxy's `ScenarioData` table says, per mission, which layers of each zone are on: a column named after the zone, holding bits. Bit 0 is `LayerA`. A zone has 32 layers now, `LayerA` to `LayerZ` then `LayerAA` to `LayerAF`, not the Wii's 16.

```text
StageData/MyGalaxy/MyGalaxyScenario.arc/scenariodata.bcsv.json
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ScenarioNo` | The mission's number |
| `PowerStarId` | The star's number in the stage |
| `IsHidden` | 1: hidden until found |
| `Comet` | `Red`, `Dark`, `Blue` etc: a comet mission |
| `<ZoneName>` | Bits: the layers of that zone on in this mission |

More than eight stars in a galaxy is fine. The star-choosing screen shows pages of six, the save keeps them all, and left and right turn the page. See [A new galaxy](#p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy).

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--a-stages-light-and-cameras"></a>

### A stage's light and cameras

Light and cameras are tables too, so a merge changes them without replacing the files.

A galaxy's lights are `ObjectData/LightData.arc/Light<Galaxy>.bcsv`, one row per light by its `AreaLightName`, and `LightData.bcsv` says which light each area of the game uses. Colours are 0 to 255 per channel, for the player, the planets, and strong and weak objects, each with a light and an ambient (`PlayerLight0ColorR`, `PlanetAmbientG`...). A table read out may show 255 as `-1`: the same value.

```text
layers/base/merge/ObjectData/LightData.arc/LightEggStarGalaxy.bcsv.json
```

```json
{ "change": [ { "where": { "AreaLightName": "[デフォルト]エッグプラネット" },
                "set": { "PlayerLight0ColorR": 255, "PlayerLight0ColorG": 140, "PlayerLight0ColorB": 60 } } ] }
```

A galaxy's cameras are `StageData/<Galaxy>.arc/camera/CameraParam.bcam`, one row per camera: its kind (`camtype`), distance (`dist`), field of view (`fovy`) and the rest.

```text
layers/base/merge/StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc/camera/CameraParam.bcam.json
```

```json
{ "change": [ { "where": { "camtype": "CAM_TYPE_XZ_PARA" }, "set": { "dist": 2600.0, "fovy": 55.0 } } ] }
```

Examples: `examples/evening-light` (Good Egg in an evening's light), `examples/far-camera` (its cameras further back and wider). `lumalink check`, given your game, tries each merge on it: it names a column the table doesn't have, and a row that matches nothing.

<a id="p-tutorials-03-levels--stage-rules"></a>

### Stage rules

Some rules go by a stage's name. To make your stage a hub, a Bowser arena or an ocean level, see [Stage rules](#p-reference-stage-rules).


<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--music-and-sound"></a>

## Music and sound

Modern files: `.wav` (16-bit PCM) or `.ogg` (Vorbis). They become the game's own form when the player applies the mod.

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--replace-a-track"></a>

### Replace a track

Put a file with the track's name in `AudioRes/Stream`:

```text
layers/base/files/AudioRes/Stream/SMG_stage_egg.ogg
```

`lumalink files AudioRes/Stream --game game.pak` lists them.

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--a-new-track"></a>

### A new track

A file and a row:

```json
"music": [{
  "name": "MyTheme",
  "file": "AudioRes/Stream/MyTheme.ogg",
  "stages": [
    { "stage": "EggStarGalaxy" },
    { "stage": "EggStarGalaxy", "scenario": 3 },
    { "stage": "EggStarGalaxy", "change_area": 1 }
  ]
}]
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Yours. Names starting `SE_`, `BGM_`, `MBGM_`, `STM_`, `ME_` are the game's |
| `file` | Its place in `files/` |
| `stage` | A stage it plays in |
| `scenario` | One mission. Left out: every mission with no row of its own |
| `change_area` | What a `ChangeBgmCube` with that `Obj_arg1` starts |

A row here comes before the game's own music for that stage, comets and fortresses included.

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--loops"></a>

### Loops

From the file: a WAV's `smpl` chunk, an Ogg's `LOOPSTART` with `LOOPEND` or `LOOPLENGTH` comments. Without them the whole track loops.

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--music-from-a-plugin"></a>

### Music from a plugin

```c
game->play_music("MyTheme");
game->stop_music(60);  /* over 60 frames */
```

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--sound-effects-from-a-file"></a>

### Sound effects from a file

A sound by its name, played from a file. A new name, or one of the game's to replace it wherever it plays:

```json
"layers": [ {
  "path": "layers/base",
  "sound_effects": [
    { "name": "SE_SY_GET_COIN", "file": "AudioRes/Stream/mycoin.wav" },
    { "name": "MyBoom", "file": "AudioRes/Stream/boom.ogg" }
  ]
} ]
```

The file goes in `files/` at that place. A game sound replaced plays the file wherever the game starts it: by its name, and by
its number too, as the player's voices are started (`SE_PV_JUMP_S`, Mario's small jump). Luigi plays the same voices: a row named
`SE_PV_JUMP_S@luigi` is played in its place while he is the player, and without one he plays the row for every player.

In a plugin, `game->play(actor, NEBULA_PLAY_SOUND, "MyBoom")` plays it from an object, and `game->play_system_sound("MyBoom")` from nowhere in particular. Game sound names are in the sound table: a level's `SoundEmitterCube`, an object's own table, and `lumalink table` on any file that names them show what's used.

<a id="p-tutorials-04-music-and-sound--the-games-sound-banks"></a>

### The game's sound banks

The Wii's sound effects are wave banks, one set per stage. With any mod on, all 53 stay loaded: an object placed away from its home stage still sounds right. To replace a bank's waves, put a file at its place in `AudioRes/Waves`, as Wii mods do.

An object's sounds come from its archive's sound table, played by the animation's action. To change which sound an action plays, change that table.


<a id="p-tutorials-05-text"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--text-and-other-languages"></a>

## Text, and other languages

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--a-message"></a>

### A message

Any message in the game, by its id, in as many languages as you like:

```json
"text": {
  "GalaxyName_EggStarGalaxy": { "default": "The Very First Galaxy", "fr": "La toute première galaxie" },
  "GalaxyNameShort_EggStarGalaxy": "First Galaxy",
  "ScenarioName_EggStarGalaxy1": "A New Start"
}
```

Any number of mods can add messages, which replacing the message files doesn't allow. Where two set one, the higher on the list wins.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--languages"></a>

### Languages

`en`, `en-GB`, `fr`, `fr-CA`, `es`, `es-MX`, `de`, `it`, `nl`, `pt`, `ja`, `ko`, `zh-Hans`, `zh-Hant`. The game takes its own language, then that language without its region, then `default`.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--the-ids"></a>

### The ids

| Id | What it is |
|---|---|
| `GalaxyName_<galaxy>` | A galaxy's name |
| `GalaxyNameShort_<galaxy>` | Its short name |
| `ScenarioName_<galaxy><n>` | A mission's name |
| Anything else | Each talk and interface message. A level's `MessageId` names its message, and the message file names them all |

To list every message in the game, open its message file: `lumalink extract LocalizeData/UsEnglish/MessageData/Message.arc --game game.pak -o out`. In a language folder such as `UsEnglish`.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--pauses-pages-colours-message-tags"></a>

### Pauses, pages, colours: message tags

Words can hold the game's own message tags, in brackets. They work in `text`, in talk lines (below) and in a plugin's words.

| Tag | Does |
|---|---|
| `[wait 30]` | Stops the text for 30 frames |
| `[page]` | Ends the box; the rest comes on the next press |
| `[center]` | Centres the line |
| `[sound SE_NAME]` | Plays one of the game's system sounds as the text reaches it |
| `[icon 7]` | Picture 7 of the game's picture font: buttons, stars, coins |
| `[small]`, `[normal]`, `[large]` | The text's size from here |
| `[player]` | The player's name: Mario or Luigi |
| `[color 1]` | The game's text colour 1 from here; `[color 0]` goes back |
| `[tag G T u...]` | Any other tag of the game: its group, its number and its parameters |

`[[` is one `[`. Anything else in brackets stays as written. A message read out with `lumalink extract` shows its tags this way, so one copied and put back is the game's own.

A new message in `text` can take the talk settings (balloon, camera, sound) of one of the game's with `like`:

```json
"text": {
  "MyNpc_Hello": { "default": "Hi, [player]!", "like": "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio012" }
}
```

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--talk-new-lines-and-what-follows-them"></a>

### Talk: new lines, and what follows them

A character's talk is lines joined by a flow: after this line, that one, or a question, or an event. A layer's `merge/MessageData/messages.json` adds lines and changes flows, in every language the game has (`merge/<Language>/MessageData/Message.arc/message.bmg.json` for one language). Any number of mods can add to it.

```json
{
  "lines": {
    "NewTalk_Ask": { "default": "Say, [player]...[wait 20] want to hear a secret?", "fr": "Dis, [player]...[wait 20] tu veux connaître un secret ?", "like": "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio012" },
    "NewTalk_Secret": { "default": "The Toad Brigade naps in shifts.[page]Don't tell the captain!", "like": "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio012" },
    "NewTalk_Later": { "default": "Suit yourself!", "like": "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio012" }
  },
  "flows": {
    "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio012": "NewTalk_Ask",
    "NewTalk_Ask": {
      "ask": "select",
      "choices": { "yes": { "default": "Yes!", "fr": "Oui !" }, "no": "Not now" },
      "yes": "NewTalk_Secret",
      "no": "NewTalk_Later"
    },
    "NewTalk_Secret": "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio013",
    "NewTalk_Later": "AstroGalaxy_Kinopio013"
  }
}
```

This is `examples/new-talk`: a Toad in the Comet Observatory asks a question of his own, then talks on as before. `examples/new-npc` gives a new character its own talk the same way.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--lines"></a>

#### Lines

A line is its words (one string for every language), or an object of words by language and its talk settings. Languages are named as in `text` (`fr-CA`, then `fr`), or by the game's folder (`UsFrench`), then `default`. A line of the game given no words in a language keeps its own there. A new line needs words for every language: give it a `default`.

| Key | Sets |
|---|---|
| `like` | A game line whose talk settings a new line starts from. Without it: an ordinary talk |
| `talk` | `normal`, `short`, `event`, `compose`, `flow` or `null` |
| `balloon` | The balloon's kind, 0 to 255 |
| `camera` | `normal`, `event` or `none` |
| `camera_set` | The stage's camera for the line, 0 to 65535 |
| `sound` | The talker's voice, -128 to 127 |
| `area` | The line's area number, as the game's lines have it, -128 to 127 |
| `already_read` | The number the game marks the line read under (see `message_read`), -128 to 127 |

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--flows"></a>

#### Flows

`flows` says, for a line by its id, what comes after it. A step is:

| Step | Means |
|---|---|
| A line's id | That line next |
| `null` | The talk ends |
| `{ "ask": ..., "yes": step, "no": step }` | A question: one step if it holds, the other if not |
| `{ "event": ..., "value": n, "next": step }` | Something happens, then `next` |

What `ask` can be:

| `ask` | Holds when |
|---|---|
| `select` | The player answers yes. `choices` gives the two answers' words; or `param` picks one of the game's 19 answer pairs (0 to 18) |
| `func` | The talker's own test, with `param` |
| `near_player` | The player is near the talker |
| `switch_a`, `switch_b` | The talker's switch is on |
| `player_normal`, `player_bee`, `player_boo` | The player is in that form |
| `player_luigi` | The player is Luigi |
| `power_star_appeared` | The stage's power star has appeared |
| `already_done` | The talker has done its part already |
| `galaxy_result` | One of the Comet Observatory's results, `param` saying which |
| `time_keep_demo` | A timed scene is running |
| `message_read` | Message-read number `param` is set |

What `event` can be:

| `event` | Does |
|---|---|
| `func`, `func_stop` | The talker's own action, with `value`; the talk waits until it is done |
| `anime` | The talker's animation `value` |
| `switch_a`, `switch_b` | Turns the talker's switch on |
| `kill` | The talker's leaving, with `value` |
| `skip` | Ends the talk at once |
| `none` | Nothing: a place for a plugin to watch |

A plugin hears each line open (`NEBULA_MOD_EVENT_TALK_LINE`, with the line's id) and each answer (`NEBULA_MOD_EVENT_TALK_CHOICE`). `lumalink check` reads the lines and flows and names what's wrong: a flow naming no line, a new line without words, an unknown `ask` or `event`, a `select` with both `choices` and `param`.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--whole-message-files"></a>

### Whole message files

A mod can replace `Message.bmg` from a language's message archive, as Wii mods do. If a mod sets text in some language folders and not the one being played, the game shows the mod's text from the same language of another region, then English, then what it has.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--a-language-the-game-doesnt-have"></a>

### A language the game doesn't have

A fan translation goes in the language players pick with least to lose, with a layer limited to it:

```json
{ "path": "layers/russian", "when": { "language": ["UsEnglish"] } }
```

Or put it in `text` under `default`. Then players of every language get it. Replace the fonts if your alphabet needs other letters: `font.brfnt` in the same places.

<a id="p-tutorials-05-text--in-a-plugin"></a>

### In a plugin

```c
game->add_text("MyMessage", "Hello!");   /* at start */
game->show_message("MyMessage", 1);      /* in play, centred */
game->hide_message();
```


<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--change-how-the-game-plays"></a>

## Change how the game plays

No code for any of this. All of it goes in a layer, so an [option](#p-tutorials-07-options) can turn any of it on.

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--tunables"></a>

### Tunables

Every tuning number in the game is a tunable, named after its source file and its name. The mod says
`"requires": ["tunables"]`, and a layer sets them:

```json
"tunables": {
  "GameRules.cPlayerHealth": 6,
  "GameRules.cLifeUpHealth": 12,
  "GameDataPlayerStatus.cMaxPlayerLeft": 999,
  "GameDataPlayerStatus.cStartingPlayerLeft": 20,
  "ScenePlayingResult.cCoinStepNum": 100,
  "ScenePlayingResult.cStarPieceStepNum": 0,
  "GameRules.cMaxCoins": 5000,
  "ScenePlayingResult.cPurpleCoinPowerStarAppearNum": 50,
  "MarioActor.cWaterAir": 16
}
```

Health can be anything: the meter's six parts show it in proportion and the number is exact. Numbers past what the game shows stay on one line. See [the game's rules and how to list every tunable](#p-reference-settings).

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--how-the-player-moves"></a>

### How the player moves

```json
"player_constants": {
  "mario": { "mJumpHeight": [null, null, 60.0] },
  "luigi": { "mJumpHeight": [null, null, 45.0] },
  "both": { "mFireModeTime": 2400, "mIceModeTime": 2400 }
}
```

Mario and Luigi each have a table of 493 numbers. The ones people reach for first:

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| `mJumpHeight` | Each kind of jump's height. 0 normal, 1 second, 2 triple |
| `mGravityJumping` | Gravity while rising, per kind of jump |
| `mJumpFrontSpeed` | Speed forward in a jump |
| `mMaxDropSpeed` | How fast the player falls |
| `mHardLandingHeight` | The fall that hurts |
| `mFireModeTime`, `mIceModeTime`, `mMetalHoldTime`, `mTornadoHoldTime`, `mRacketHoldTime` | How long each power-up lasts, in frames |

[All of them](#p-reference-player-numbers), with what each table has.

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--which-objects-exist"></a>

### Which objects exist

One of the game's objects becomes another, or is gone, wherever the game makes it.

```json
"object_changes": [
  { "object": "RestartCube" },
  { "object": "BenefitItemLifeUp", "becomes": "BenefitItemOneUp" },
  { "object": "KinokoLifeUp", "becomes": "KinokoOneUp", "in": "treasure_boxes" },
  { "object": "KinokoLifeUp", "becomes": "KinokoOneUp", "in": "display_models" }
]
```

Removing `RestartCube` removes every checkpoint in the game. See [`luma.json`](#p-reference--object-changes).

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--comets"></a>

### Comets

```json
"comet_time_limits": [ { "galaxy": "BattleShipGalaxy", "mission": 4, "seconds": 150 } ],
"comet_schedule": [ { "dome": 2, "comets": [ { "galaxy": "BattleShipGalaxy", "coins": 1 } ] } ]
```

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--what-opens-what"></a>

### What opens what

Event flags are the game's progression: what each dome needs, what each hungry Luma costs. See [A new galaxy](#p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--the-games-progression).

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--rules-that-go-by-a-stages-name"></a>

### Rules that go by a stage's name

```json
"stages": [ { "stage": "OceanRingGalaxy", "own_rules": false } ]
```

Takes the swim-angle limit off the ocean. See [Stage rules](#p-reference-stage-rules).

<a id="p-tutorials-06-rules-and-physics--one-thing-to-keep-in-mind"></a>

### One thing to keep in mind

A mod that changes what's needed to reach things is a different journey through the game: give it its own saves with `"save": { "mode": "own" }`.


<a id="p-tutorials-07-options"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-07-options--give-players-options"></a>

## Give players options

<a id="p-tutorials-07-options--choices"></a>

### Choices

```json
"options": [{
  "id": "difficulty",
  "name": "Difficulty",
  "description": "How hard it hits",
  "default": "normal",
  "choices": [
    { "id": "normal", "name": "Normal" },
    { "id": "hard", "name": "Hard" }
  ]
}],
"layers": [
  { "path": "layers/base" },
  { "when": { "option": { "difficulty": ["hard"] } }, "tunables": { "MarioActor.cHitTakesAll": true } }
]
```

Players choose on the Mods page. The choice lasts through updates to the mod. `off` as a choice's id is shown in the player's own language and means this adds nothing.

<a id="p-tutorials-07-options--numbers"></a>

### Numbers

A range is a choice for each number:

```json
"options": [{
  "id": "health", "name": "Health", "default": 6,
  "range": { "from": 1, "to": 20, "step": 1 }
}],
"layers": [{
  "tunables": { "GameRules.cPlayerHealth": { "option": "health" } },
  "player_constants": { "both": { "mFireModeTime": { "option": "fire-time" } } }
}]
```

A tunable or a player number takes the chosen number directly, with no layer per value.

<a id="p-tutorials-07-options--when"></a>

### `when`

A layer is used when all of its `when` hold.

| Key | Holds when |
|---|---|
| `version` | The game is one of these: `["E", "P", "J", "K", "W", "C"]` |
| `language` | The language folder being played is one of these: `["UsEnglish", "EuFrench"]` |
| `platform` | The device is one of `windows`, `android`, `linux`, `macos`, `ios` |
| `option` | Each named option is on one of its listed choices |
| `mods` | Each of these mods is on: a patch that makes two mods work together |
| `not` | This isn't so. One `when`, or a list of them, none of which may hold |
| `any` | A list of `when`: one of them holds |

```json
{ "path": "layers/with-green-stars", "when": { "mods": ["green-stars"], "not": { "platform": ["android"] } } }
```

A key this Nebula doesn't know makes it false, so a mod made for a later version loses the layer rather than breaking.

<a id="p-tutorials-07-options--anything-can-be-switched"></a>

### Anything can be switched

Everything a mod can say at its top level can also go in a layer: `text`, `music`, `galaxies`, `event_flags`, `comet_schedule`, `story`. So an option can turn on a new galaxy, a soundtrack or a translation.

<a id="p-tutorials-07-options--in-a-plugin"></a>

### In a plugin

```c
const char* mode = game->option(me, "difficulty");  /* its choice's id */
```

A plugin's own row can have a `when` as a layer does: only its code for that choice runs.


<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--a-new-object-without-code"></a>

## A new object, without code

A new name that levels can place, behaving as one of the game's objects, with its own model.

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--1-choose-what-it-behaves-as"></a>

### 1. Choose what it behaves as

[Objects](#p-reference-objects) lists everything. For a platform that just sits there, `FloaterLandPartsFrame` is a plain map object. For a Goomba with a new look, `Kuribo`.

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--2-say-so"></a>

### 2. Say so

```json
"layers": [ {
  "path": "layers/base",
  "object_classes": [ { "name": "BigStoneBlock", "like": "FloaterLandPartsFrame" } ]
} ]
```

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--3-give-it-files"></a>

### 3. Give it files

Its files are `ObjectData/<name>.arc`:

```text
layers/base/files/ObjectData/BigStoneBlock.arc/BigStoneBlock.glb
layers/base/files/ObjectData/BigStoneBlock.arc/BigStoneBlock.kcl.glb
```

If the object it's like asks for a model by its own name (a `Kuribo` asks for `Kuribo`), it gets yours instead. Animations are asked for by name: copy the original's names, with `lumalink files ObjectData/Kuribo.arc --game game.pak` to see them. Its joints too, where the original's code holds something by a joint (a Goomba's `Head`).

What your archive doesn't have comes from the original's:

| Missing from yours | What happens |
|---|---|
| A table (`actoranimctrl.bcsv`, `storydemoshadow.bcsv`, ...) | The original's is read |
| A sound animation (`walk.bas`: footsteps on frames) | The original's plays with your animation of that name |
| Effects (no `AutoEffectList` row for your name) | The original's: a squashed Bramblet gives off a Goomba's puff |
| An animation the code plays | Nothing plays for it, and nothing breaks: a model with no colour animations (`.brk`) is still a Toad |

An animation standing for one of the original's plays as that one does: once (a Goomba's `FlatDown`), or looping (`Walk`). The code waits for the end of those it plays once, so this matters. To say it yourself, see [models](#p-tutorials-02-models--how-an-animation-plays).

`examples/new-galaxy` makes a new enemy this way: `Bramblet`, like `Kuribo`, its model and 28 animations from one glTF file.

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--4-place-it"></a>

### 4. Place it

```text
layers/base/merge/StageData/EggStarGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo.json
```

```json
{ "rows": [ {
  "name": "BigStoneBlock", "l_id": 3200,
  "pos_x": -2200, "pos_y": -12700, "pos_z": -14500,
  "dir_x": 0, "dir_y": 0, "dir_z": 0, "scale_x": 1, "scale_y": 1, "scale_z": 1,
  "Obj_arg0": -1, "Obj_arg1": -1, "Obj_arg2": -1, "Obj_arg3": -1,
  "Obj_arg4": -1, "Obj_arg5": -1, "Obj_arg6": -1, "Obj_arg7": -1,
  "SW_A": -1, "SW_B": -1, "SW_APPEAR": -1, "SW_DEAD": -1, "SW_SLEEP": -1,
  "CommonPath_ID": -1, "ClippingGroupId": -1, "GroupId": -1, "DemoGroupId": -1,
  "MapParts_ID": -1, "ViewGroupId": -1, "CameraSetId": -1, "CastId": -1,
  "MessageId": -1, "ShapeModelNo": -1
} ] }
```

The player stands on it, and it draws, sounds and counts as what it's like.

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--what-it-can-and-cant-change"></a>

### What it can and can't change

The look, the shape, the sounds in its archive and any table in its archive are yours, and so are effects given in an `AutoEffectList` row of its name. What it does is the original's. Its arguments mean what the original's do. For behaviour of its own, [a plugin](#p-tutorials-10-first-plugin) makes a new object in a few lines.

<a id="p-tutorials-08-new-objects--if-a-file-is-missing"></a>

### If a file is missing

With any mod on, a level placing an object whose archive isn't there leaves that object out, and the log says so. The level goes on.


<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--a-new-galaxy"></a>

## A new galaxy

A galaxy beside the game's is its files and a row.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--the-files"></a>

### The files

```text
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy/MyGalaxyScenario.arc    its missions and zones
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc                     its main zone
layers/base/files/StageData/MyPlanetZone.arc                 any other zones
```

Levels come from a level editor such as Whitehole. You can also start from one of the game's: `lumalink extract StageData/EggStarGalaxy --game game.pak -o out` writes the scenario's tables as JSON.

`examples/new-galaxy` is a whole one, every file written by `source/make_galaxy.py`: a planet, a new enemy, two missions, a cutscene and a theme.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--a-zones-tables-as-json"></a>

#### A zone's tables as JSON

Each of the zone's placement tables can be JSON, at its path with `.json` added:

```text
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc/jmp/start/common/startinfo.json          where the player starts
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc/jmp/list/stageinfo.json
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo.json        objects in every mission
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/planetobjinfo.json  gravity
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/layera/objinfo.json        objects in layer A's missions
layers/base/files/StageData/MyGalaxy.arc/camera/cameraparam.bcam.json             cameras, if any
```

A table is its rows. A column whose numbers have fractions is a float on its own; one whose values all happen to be whole says so in `columns`:

```json
{ "columns": { "pos_x": "float", "pos_y": "float", "pos_z": "float" },
  "rows": [ { "name": "Kuribo", "l_id": 10, "pos_x": 0, "pos_y": 1510, "pos_z": 0 } ] }
```

A column nobody has a name for is written by its hash, as `lumalink extract` writes it: `"0xe4ef3738": "Normal"`. A zone without cameras uses the game's default camera.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--a-planet"></a>

#### A planet

A planet is a model with solid ground, `ObjectData/MyPlanet.arc/MyPlanet.glb` and `MyPlanet.kcl.glb` ([models](#p-tutorials-02-models)), placed in `objinfo` by its name. The game makes planets of the names in `ObjectData/PlanetMapDataTable.arc/PlanetMapDataTable.bcsv`, so add a row:

```text
layers/base/merge/ObjectData/PlanetMapDataTable.arc/PlanetMapDataTable.bcsv.json
```

```json
{ "rows": [ { "PlanetName": "MyPlanet", "LowFlag": 0, "MiddleFlag": 0, "BloomFlag": 0, "WaterFlag": 0, "IndirectFlag": 0 } ] }
```

The flags say it has other models of its own beside it (`MyPlanetBloom`, `MyPlanetWater`, ...). Its pull is a gravity in `planetobjinfo`: `GlobalPointGravity` at its middle pulls towards it, as far out as its `Range`.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--missions"></a>

#### Missions

`MyGalaxyScenario.arc` holds `ScenarioData.bcsv`, one row per mission, and `ZoneList.bcsv`, one row per zone. Either can be `.bcsv.json`:

```json
{ "rows": [
  { "ScenarioNo": 1, "PowerStarId": 1, "MyGalaxy": 1, "ErrorCheck": 1, "IsHidden": 0, "Comet": "", "AppearPowerStarObj": "" },
  { "ScenarioNo": 2, "PowerStarId": 2, "MyGalaxy": 3, "ErrorCheck": 1, "IsHidden": 0, "Comet": "", "AppearPowerStarObj": "" }
] }
```

The column named after each zone holds that mission's layers, as bits: 1 is layer A, 2 layer B, 3 both.

There's no limit of eight stars. A galaxy with more shows six at a time on its star screen, with the page beside its name; left and right turn it, as does pressing at either side of the screen. The save keeps them all.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--the-row"></a>

### The row

```json
"galaxies": [{
  "name": "MyGalaxy",
  "dome": 1,
  "map_position": [-60, -100],
  "stars_to_open": 0,
  "open_conditions": [],
  "hungry_luma": { "slot": 7, "star_bits": 400 }
}],
"save": { "mode": "own" },
"text": {
  "GalaxyName_MyGalaxy": "My Galaxy",
  "GalaxyNameShort_MyGalaxy": "My Galaxy",
  "ScenarioName_MyGalaxy1": "The First Star"
}
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | Its folder's name |
| `dome` | Its dome, 1 to 6, or up to 16: see below. 0: the grand map |
| `map_position` | `[right, up]` from the middle of its dome's page, which is 608 by 456. The game makes the icon |
| `map_pane` | A pane of `MapGrandGalaxy` showing it, instead |
| `stars_to_open` | Power stars it takes |
| `open_conditions` | Up to three event flags |
| `hungry_luma` | The Luma that opens it: place a `TicoGalaxy` with its `Obj_arg7` at `slot`. The game's are 0 to 6. `star_bits` is the price |

A galaxy needs its own saves, as a save's shape follows the list of galaxies. `lumalink check` tells you if you forget.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--getting-there"></a>

### Getting there

A hungry Luma, a launch star, or a plugin: `game->change_stage("MyGalaxy", 1)`, or `game->open_scenario_select("MyGalaxy")` for its star screen.

To place the Luma in the Observatory:

```text
layers/base/merge/StageData/AstroGalaxy.arc/jmp/placement/common/objinfo.json
```

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--the-games-progression"></a>

### The game's progression

```json
"event_flags": [
  { "name": "ExOpen1CocoonExGalaxy", "kind": 3, "a": 1, "b": 0, "first": "SandClockGalaxy" },
  { "name": "StarPieceCocoonExGalaxy", "kind": 8, "a": 5, "b": 80, "first": "CocoonExGalaxy" },
  { "name": "PowerStarComplete", "kind": 1, "a": 186 }
]
```

A name the game has is changed, a new one added. The numbers go past the Wii's 255.

| Kind | The row says | `a`, `b` | `first`, `second` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many stars | `a`: the number | |
| 2 | A galaxy's stars to open it | | `first`: the galaxy |
| 3 | A special star was got | `a`: which | `first`: its galaxy |
| 4 | Two other rows are both on | | `first`, `second`: the rows |
| 8 | A hungry Luma | `a`: slot. `b`: price | `first`: what it opens |

Where galaxies are on the map and their star counts are the table `NebulaData/GalaxyInfoTable.bcsv` (or `.bcsv.json`), which a layer can replace or edit through `merge/`. So is `NebulaData/StoryProgressTable.bcsv`.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--stars"></a>

### Stars

A star's number comes from `PowerStarId` and the mission, as a `PowerStar` placed in the mission's layer or an object that gives one. Green and red stars, Luigi's stars and grand stars are `event_flags` rows named `SpecialStarGreen`, `SpecialStarRed`, `SpecialStarFindingLuigi` and `SpecialStarGrand`, of kind 3.

The total isn't fixed at 121. `PowerStarComplete` is only a row: set it to what your mod has.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--domes-past-six"></a>

### Domes past six

`dome` goes to 16, and `comet_schedule` with it. A dome past six is built by you: its hub objects (`AstroDome`, `AstroDomeEntrance`, `AstroDomeSky`, `AstroStarPlate`) take their dome from `Obj_arg0` and their model by its number, as `ObjectData/AstroDomeEntrance7.arc`. Comets past the sixth dome aren't kept in the save, and start over each play. It has no icon on the grand map unless you give it one with `map_pane`.

<a id="p-tutorials-09-new-galaxy--your-own-journey"></a>

### Your own journey

To start at your galaxy instead of the game's prologue: [A total conversion](#p-tutorials-16-total-conversion).


<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin"></a>

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--your-first-plugin"></a>

## Your first plugin

A plugin is a native library that the game loads and calls directly. It isn't sandboxed: it can do what the game can do. It's fast, and it's the way to behaviour no table can describe. Players are asked before it first runs.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--start-one"></a>

### Start one

```console
lumalink new "My Mod" --plugin
cd "My Mod"
```

You get `source/plugin.c`, `build.cmd` and `plugins/`. You need [clang](https://releases.llvm.org/) and nothing else: a plugin using only this interface needs no C library and no game files.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--the-smallest-one"></a>

### The smallest one

```c
#include <nebula_mod_api.h>

static const NebulaModApi* game;
static const NebulaPlugin* me;

/* Runs once, before the game starts. */
NEBULA_PLUGIN_ENTRY(api, self) {
    game = api;
    me = self;
    game->log(me, "hello");
}
```

```console
lumalink build .
```

That builds the plugin for all eight devices from the one computer, with clang and its linker (lld) and no C library, and names every library in luma.json:

```json
"plugins": [{ "api": 2, "binaries": { "windows-x64": "plugins/my-mod-windows-x64.dll", "android-arm64": "plugins/my-mod-android-arm64.so", "...": "..." } }]
```

Devices: `windows-x64`, `windows-arm64`, `linux-x64`, `linux-arm64`, `macos-x64`, `macos-arm64`, `android-arm64`, `android-x64`. `lumalink check` names any device a plugin has no library for; on that device the game says THIS MOD HAS NO VERSION FOR THIS DEVICE. A plugin's row takes a `when` as a layer does.

With no C library there's no `malloc` or `printf`: the interface has them. `game->alloc(bytes)` and `game->release(p)` for memory, `game->format(buffer, size, "%d coins", n)` for text, `game->log` to write it. If the linker stops on `memcpy` or `memset` (clang makes a large copy or clear into one), define it in your source.

`game->log` writes to the game's log, with your mod's name on the line.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--events"></a>

### Events

The game calls you when something happens. An event nobody subscribed to costs nothing.

```c
/* Any hit is the last one. */
static int32_t stage_frame(const NebulaModEventData* data, void* user) {
    (void)user;
    if (game->value(NEBULA_VALUE_LIFE) > 1) {
        game->set_value(NEBULA_SET_LIFE, 1);
    }
    return data->value;
}

NEBULA_PLUGIN_ENTRY(api, self) {
    game = api;
    game->subscribe(NEBULA_MOD_EVENT_STAGE_FRAME, stage_frame, 0);
}
```

Return `data->value` to change nothing. For the events that ask, what you return is used: return 0 from `PLAYER_DAMAGE` to refuse a hit.

| `NEBULA_MOD_EVENT_` | When | `value` | You return |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FRAME` | Every frame, menus too | | |
| `STAGE_FRAME` | Every frame of a stage, before objects move | | |
| `STAGE_START` | A stage starts. `name`: the stage | Its mission | |
| `STAGE_END` | It's ending. Every actor and layout of it goes after this. `name`: the stage | | |
| `PLAYER_DAMAGE` | About to lose health | 1 | 0 refuses the hit |
| `PLAYER_MISS` | About to die | How (0 a fall out of the level) | -1 refuses it: move the player somewhere safe yourself |
| `PLAYER_SPIN` | A spin starts | | |
| `PLAYER_JUMP` | Leaves the ground in a jump | | |
| `PLAYER_LAND` | Lands | | |
| `POWER_UP` | The power-up is about to change | The new one | Used instead |
| `COIN` | Coins about to be added | How many | Added instead |
| `STAR_BIT` | Star bits about to be added | How many | Added instead |
| `STAR_GET` | A star is won. `name`: the galaxy | Its number | |
| `POWER_STAR_APPEAR` | A star comes into the stage | Its number | |
| `CUTSCENE_START`, `CUTSCENE_END` | `name`: the cutscene | | |
| `ACTOR_APPEAR`, `ACTOR_KILL` | Any object. `actor`, `name` | | |
| `PAUSE` | The pause menu | 1 open, 0 closed | |
| `GAME_SAVE` | About to write the save | | |
| `TALK_LINE` | A line of talk opens. `actor`: who talks. `name`: the line's message id | | |
| `TALK_CHOICE` | The player answered a yes/no question. `actor`, `name`: the question | 1 yes, 0 no | |
| `CUTSCENE_PART` | A part of a cutscene starts. `name`: the part | Its number, from 0 | |
| `CAMERA_CHANGE` | The camera changes. `name`: its id in the stage's camera table | 0 an area's, 1 an event's | |
| `SOUND_START` | A sound effect is about to start. `name`: the sound | Its number | The sound that plays; -1 for none |
| `EFFECT_START` | An object starts an effect. `actor`, `name`: the effect | | |
| `SCREEN` | A screen layout is shown or goes away. `name`: the layout | 1 shown, 0 gone | |
| `ACTOR_MESSAGE` | An object gets an attack, stomp, push or grab. `actor`: who gets it. `name`: the message | The message | -1 refuses it |
| `PLAYER_ACTION` | The player starts a swim, hang, slide, fall and so on | The action | |

`SOUND_START`, `EFFECT_START` and `ACTOR_MESSAGE` call you for every sound, effect or message while you're subscribed; subscribe to them only when you use them. The game's [EVENTS.md](#p-reference-events) lists every message and action number.

Subscribing happens only in `nebula_plugin_start`, as do `register_object`, `hook` and the row calls (`add_*`, `set_stage_rules`, `set_object_class`, `set_story` and so on).

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--the-player"></a>

### The player

```c
NebulaActor* player = game->player();   /* null between stages and on the file select screen */
float at[3];
game->get_position(player, at);
game->value(NEBULA_VALUE_COINS);
game->set_value(NEBULA_SET_POWER_UP, NEBULA_POWER_UP_FIRE);   /* any power-up, anywhere */
game->jump_player(velocity);
game->set_player_control(0);
if (game->buttons_pressed() & NEBULA_BUTTON_JUMP) { ... }
game->set_player_constant(0, "mJumpHeight", 0, 40.0f);        /* any number, at any time */
```

Buttons, whatever device they're on: `NEBULA_BUTTON_JUMP`, `SPIN`, `CROUCH`, `CAMERA`, `FIRE`, `DPAD_UP`, `DPAD_DOWN`, `DPAD_LEFT`, `DPAD_RIGHT`, `PAUSE`, `MAP`. `stick(&x, &y)` and `pointer(xy)` read the rest.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--things-in-the-world"></a>

### Things in the world

```c
NebulaActor* coin = game->spawn("Coin", at);                 /* any object, on any stage */
for (NebulaActor* a = game->find_actor("Kuribo", 0); a; a = game->find_actor("Kuribo", a)) {
    game->attack_actor(a, 0, NEBULA_ATTACK_STOMP);           /* every Goomba */
}
NebulaActor* near[32];
int count = game->actors_near(at, 1000.0f, near, 32);
game->raycast(from, to, hit);
game->gravity_at(at, down);
game->is_in_area("WaterCube", at);
```

`spawn` loads what it needs. An object that can't exist away from a level's placement answers null.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--kept-across-plays"></a>

### Kept across plays

```c
game->store_set(me, "best", 12);
int best = game->store_get(me, "best", 0);
game->store_set_text(me, "name", "Rosalina");
```

Per mod, in the settings folder, beside the player's saves. Saved at once.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--everything-else"></a>

### Everything else

[The whole interface](#p-reference-plugin-api) lists all 167 calls: animations, switches, rails, cameras, cutscenes, music, movies, messages, saves. Past that, the [game's own headers and hooks](#p-reference--13-plugins-the-games-headers-and-hooks) reach any function.

<a id="p-tutorials-10-first-plugin--examples"></a>

### Examples

| Example | What it shows |
|---|---|
| [`one-health`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/one-health) | Reading and setting the player's state |
| [`coin-kills`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/coin-kills) | Events |
| [`achievements`](https://github.com/keepvaibin/lumalink/blob/main/examples/achievements) | The mod's own achievements |
